label: Identity
quote:
R E V I E W A R T I C L E
Stimulating Natural Regeneration of Tropical Forest
on Degraded Land: Approaches, Outcomes, and
Information Gaps
Luke P. Shoo1,2 and Carla P. Catterall3
disposition: Title/authors/venue/DOI checked; preserve historic ID, actual authors Shoo/Catterall not Holl.

label: Abstract
quote:
Abstract
Extensive land clearing in many parts of the global tropics
is a major threat to biodiversity, and strategies are urgently
needed to reinstate forest. Tree planting is a commonly
used strategy to rapidly restore forest to degraded land-
scapes. However, tree planting is expensive, and in most
cases ﬁnancial constraints prevent its use at a scale needed
to address the ongoing legacy of land clearing. Here,
we conduct a quantitative review of literature from the
global tropics and evaluate outcomes of less intensive inter-
ventions (i.e. non-planting) aimed at stimulating natural
regeneration of forest. We focus speciﬁcally on overcom-
ing barriers to native plant regeneration that predominate
in the earliest stages of succession. Common interventions
include varied strategies to suppress herbaceous vegeta-
tion (e.g. cutting or herbicide treatment), and measures to
bolster propagule supply (e.g. direct seeding and artiﬁcial
bird perches). There was an apparent trend among pair-
wise comparisons of effect sizes to suggest that combined
interventions to simultaneously suppress herbaceous vege-
tation and increase propagule supply resulted in the most
consistent outcomes in terms of promoting progress toward
restoring forest structure. Despite an obvious demand for
lower cost interventions, a paucity of information means
that it is still premature to generalize outcomes of speciﬁc
interventions and their overall cost relative to active tree
planting. Nevertheless, we report an increase in research
effort in this area, and suggest promising directions to
accelerate progress that will improve capacity to select
optimal, cost effective strategies that achieve long-term
restoration objectives with a particular level of certainty.
Key words: artiﬁcial perch, cost, direct seeding, ecological
barriers, pasture conversion, regrowth, restoration.
disposition: Duplicates body findings; no independent vote. Combined interventions improve early regeneration in scoped studies, not general establishment thresholds.

label: Introduction forest loss
quote:
Introduction
Approximately half of the tropical forest biome has been
subjected to some form of land clearing (Asner et al. 2009),
generating signiﬁcant carbon emissions, depleting important
ecosystem services (e.g. ﬂood mitigation), and threatening
global biodiversity (Bradshaw et al. 2008; van der Werf
et al. 2009). Restoration is urgently needed to reverse human
damage and prevent ongoing attrition of species from isolated
remnants (Martinez-Garza & Howe 2003). Restoration of large
areas of former agricultural land in particular is likely to be
required as transformation of forests to agriculture has been
the main source of forest conversion in the tropics—at a rate
of 3.1 million hectares per year (Achard et al. 2002).
disposition: Motivation and historical land conversion, not applicability gate.

quote:
In some tropical areas, agricultural land is being aban-
doned, and secondary succession has already begun return-
ing some form of forest to degraded landscapes (Aide et al.

1995; Letcher & Chazdon 2009). However, the rate of nat-
ural forest recovery from human disturbance is notoriously
variable, and in many cases abandoned land can remain in a
state of arrested early succession for extended periods (Corlett
1991; Cohen et al. 1995; Hooper et al. 2005). Tree plant-
ing is the most commonly used strategy to reinstate forest
(Rodrigues et al. 2009; Holl 2012). If done well, plant-
ings designed for ecological restoration can yield rapid and
predictable beneﬁts, including canopy closure, structural com-
plexity, increased richness, and biotic composition approx-
imating that found in undisturbed forest (Rodrigues et al.
2009). However, replanting forest can be expensive (Catter-
all & Harrison 2006). Since ﬁnancial cost is a major factor
impeding landscape-level restoration of high-diversity for-
est on degraded land in the tropics (Parrotta et al. 1997;
Rodrigues et al. 2009), there is a need to identify alternative
restoration techniques that require lower inputs of labor and
resources.

label: Introduction ANR methods
quote:
Less intensive restoration approaches include assisted nat-
ural regeneration (Dugan et al. 2003; Shono et al. 2007)
and rehabilitation of woody regrowth dominated by native
(Chazdon 2008; Putz & Redford 2009) or exotic trees and
shrubs (Woodford 2000; Kanowski et al. 2008; Sanger et al.
2008).

label: Introduction barriers
quote:
However, adoption of these approaches is dependent on the
presence of established trees which, in many cases, are absent
due to barriers to natural regeneration, including seed supply,
competition with grasses or other herbaceous vegetation, and
availability of microsites for germination and establishment
(Holl 2007, 2012). In such situations, interventions aimed at
overcoming barriers to native plant regeneration that predomi-
nate in the earliest stages of succession are likely to be required
(Hardwick et al. 2004; Shono et al. 2007; Chazdon 2008).
Despite an obvious need for practical and cost effective meth-
ods for “kick-starting” forest regeneration (Kelm et al. 2008),
this remains an understudied area of restoration science.
disposition: Established trees/propagules/microsites/competition describe succession feasibility, cited Holl2007/2012 and Shono2007. Rootstock/planting-material details M6; no distance direction derived from generic landscape mention.

label: Research scope
quote:
To address this deﬁciency, we review the published litera-
ture, focusing on potentially less intensive interventions aimed
at fast-tracking natural regeneration of tropical forest. We ask
the following three questions:
1. What potential strategies are available to stimulate natural
regeneration and recover tropical forest, which do not rely
on tree planting?
2. What is the relative efﬁcacy of different strategies in terms
of restoring the diversity and structure of pre-clearing
forest?
3. Do we know enough about the likely cost and long-term
trajectory of low level interventions to support decision
making aimed at optimizing cost effectiveness of restoration
projects?
We also identify important knowledge gaps and method-
ological deﬁciencies to inform directions of future research.
For simplicity and clarity, we restrict our focus to a sin-
gle but dominant problem: restoration of forest to land,
which had experienced an agricultural phase (cropland or
pasture), was then retired from agriculture, and which
subsequently remained dominated by grass or herbaceous
vegetation.
disposition: Deliberately selected disused agricultural land dominated by herbs; inclusion restriction, not universal land-cover exclusion.

label: Literature search criteria
quote:
Methods
Literature Search
Multiple search strategies were used to generate a cumulative
list of publications that quantitatively evaluated outcomes of
interventions applicable to restoring forest on degraded land
in the tropics. The core strategy involved keyword searches
in Thomson Reuters Web of Science. Search terms evolved
from reviewing terminology used in literature, and making
active judgments to reﬁne searches to locate studies that
conformed to speciﬁc criteria (see below). The following
search terms were used: restor* AND tropic* AND (barrier*
or cost or direct seed* or soil transpos* or perch*). Keyword
searches were then supplemented by reviewing references
cited by relevant studies and tracking post-publication citations
of parent articles. The accumulated list of publications was
then systematically screened for content, and articles were
retained if they met six criteria: (1) evaluated outcomes of
experimental manipulation of forest regeneration on tropical
land; (2) focused on cases where forest had been cleared
AND there had been a subsequent period of land use for
agriculture (e.g. cropping or grazing) likely to have depleted
the availability of native woody plant propagules within the
site (i.e. soil seed bank, resprouting rootstock, and existing
seedlings); (3) focused on cases where existing vegetation
was dominated by pasture grasses, dense ferns, or other
herbaceous vegetation with few woody plants; (4) considered
interventions other than direct planting of trees, seedlings,
or vegetative stakes; (5) conducted replicated comparisons
between different interventions or combinations thereof; and
(6) presented data in a form that enabled the extraction of both
means and variances of quantitative indicators of the outcomes
of interventions.
disposition: Explicit search and six study inclusion rules; not ecological establishment criteria.

label: Biome/context coding
quote:
To facilitate interpretation of the data and identify data gaps
across studies, we also compiled information on the ecoregion
(Olson et al. 2001), forest biome (rain forest = areas receiving
>1500 mm annual precipitation and dry forest = areas receiv-
ing <1500 mm annual precipitation; Whitmore 1998), the type
of past human disturbance (intensive horticulture or pasture for
livestock or slash and burn agriculture), as well as an estimate
of the duration and spatial extent of the experiment. The latter
was simply a summed area of all treatment and control plots
described in the experimental design.
disposition: Rainforest >1500mm / dryforest <1500mm (Whitmore1998) is classification, not ANR rainfall threshold. MAP/MAT/disturbance/area used as study metadata, not suitability model.

label: Study synthesis scope
quote:
The full set of papers that met our criteria provided the
foundation for a synthetic overview of experimental studies.
For a subset of papers, we also compiled quantitative estimates
of outcomes of different interventions in order to compare their
effectiveness.
disposition: Subset eligible for controlled comparisons; full list20 vs controlled10 distinguished.

label: Effect methods
quote:
Effect Sizes
Whenever feasible, measures of vegetation outcomes were
conﬁgured into pair-wise comparisons between different inter-
ventions. To avoid the potential confounding effect of different
starting conditions, we only evaluated those paired compar-
isons (and hence also studies) that possessed an unmanipulated
control (i.e. starting state with no intervention).
We classiﬁed single and combined interventions into three
broad categories according to whether they were likely
to affect (1) arrival of propagules to the site (hereafter,
“propagule supply”); or (2) processes that inﬂuence estab-
lishment, survival, or growth of trees (e.g. competition from
herbaceous vegetation, physical, and chemical properties of
soil—hereafter “ground conditions”; or (3) both. For each
intervention, we compiled estimates of the mean and stan-
dard deviation of all response variables that provided some
measure of successional trajectory (e.g. biomass of seed
rain, density of woody plants). Data were either taken
directly from values reported in the text or extracted from
ﬁgures using DataThief (B. Tummers, 2006, DataThief III,
http://datathief.org/). Response variables were then classiﬁed
into one of three metrics depending on whether they described
the impact of interventions on (1) propagule supply (e.g.
arrival of animal dispersed seed); (2) forest structure (e.g.
density/height/basal area of woody stems and ground/canopy
cover); or (3) richness (e.g. observed species richness of woody
plants).

label: Effect-size sign convention
quote:
For each pair-wise comparison, we calculated effect size as
Hedges’ g, the difference between the unmanipulated control
group and intervention treatment group means, standardized
using the pooled standard deviation of the two groups (Boren-
stein et al. 2009). We followed the meta-analytical approach of
Gibson et al. (2011), and used a conversion factor J (Boren-
stein et al. 2009) to compute a bias-corrected metric of pop-
ulation effect size, g*. We deﬁned effect sizes as positive for
comparisons where a difference in the measure of vegeta-
tion outcomes (comparison of the intervention treatment vs.
an unmanipulated control) was judged to indicate favorable
progress toward realizing the goal of restoring forest diversity
and function (e.g. increases in seed supply, woody vegetation
cover, or richness of woody species). Effect sizes were deemed
to be negative where the direction of the response was con-
sidered to impede such progress (e.g. increased biomass of
vigorous pasture grasses).
disposition: Hedges g* signed by progress toward restoration goal, not automatically sign of canonical outcome variable. Future effect lane must decode individual response variables before use.

label: Dependence handling
quote:
Some papers reported outcomes of particular interventions
for multiple response variables, or for the same response
variable across multiple sites or species. The resulting potential
for nonindependence among some pair-wise comparisons was
addressed in two ways. First, for each study we derived
a mean estimate of Hedges, g* aggregated according to
metric (propagule supply, forest structure, and richness) and
response variable (e.g. density of stems and canopy cover).
This effectively collapsed data within studies where the same
pair-wise comparison was conducted on multiple species or
reported separately for multiple sites. Second, we differentiated
between effect sizes arising from different metrics, response
variables, and studies in all subsequent representations of the
data. The decision not to aggregate intervention treatment
outcomes across all response variables enables a quantitative
synthesis of available data rather than a formal meta-analysis,
given small sample sizes in our data set.
disposition: Within-study metric/response aggregation, not formal pooled meta-analysis; repeated study outcomes not independent votes.

label: Study distribution
quote:
Results
Characteristics of Studies
Most articles described manipulative small-scale experiments
designed to understand mechanistic barriers to forest regener-
ation. Some provided information derived directly from prac-
tical trials of potential interventions. Twenty articles satisﬁed
the selection criteria for quantitative analysis (Table 1). These
studies were predominantly from the Neotropics (n = 12) but
also included Oceania (n = 2), Indo-Malay (n = 4), and Aus-
tralasia (n = 2) with no studies from the Afrotropics (Fig. 1).
Six studies (30%) were undertaken in dry forest and 14
(70%) in rain forest. The spatial extent of manipulative
experiments ranged from 0.0018 to 29.8 ha (mean = 4.9 ha;
median = 0.5 ha).
disposition: 20 articles;12 Neotropic,2Oceania,4Indo-Malay,2Australasia; noAfrotropics.6dry14rain. Area0.0018–29.8ha descriptive (Table1 rounds0.002).

label: Intervention definitions
quote:
Most interventions that manipulated ground conditions were
aimed at suppressing herbaceous vegetation either directly
(cutting, pulling, herbicide, or burning) or occasionally indi-
rectly through low-intensity grazing. Exceptions included
fertilizer addition and tilling of soil. Interventions aimed at
overcoming barriers to propagule supply comprised direct
seeding and installation of artiﬁcial bird perches. In some
cases, primary interventions were followed by secondary treat-
ments, which involved a full or partial repeat of actions
undertaken in the primary intervention. In all cases, secondary
treatments were intended to prolong suppression of herba-
ceous vegetation (e.g. spot herbicide, hand weeding, and low-
intensity grazing) or altered chemical properties of soil (i.e.
fertilizer addition). Neither burning nor mechanical tilling of
soil were used as secondary treatment options.
disposition: Cut/pull/herbicide/burn/graze/fertilize/till vsseed/perch, primary/secondary treatments. Mechanism taxonomy, not T4 criteria.

label: Propagule outcomes
quote:
Effect Sizes
Propagule Supply.
Two studies monitoring artiﬁcial perches
(ID7, 18; Table 1) indicate that perches served to increase the
number and biomass of seed introduced to a site (Fig. 2).
disposition: Two studies ID7/18 perches increase seed number/biomass. Effect pointer; neither measured establishment suitability nor distance relationship.

label: Forest-structure outcomes
quote:
Forest Structure.
The effects of interventions aimed exclu-
sively at altering ground conditions to improve forest structure
were highly variable. In a few cases, treatments had negative
consequences (Fig. 2). Efforts aimed exclusively at suppress-
ing herbaceous vegetation had limited effectiveness in return-
ing structure to dry forest (cutting, herbicide, pulling, ID1, 2,
and 13; Table 1) but responses were more positive for rain for-
est (cutting, low-intensity grazing, ID8, 10, and 16), with the
exception of burning (ID12; Table 1). Promotion of propagule
supply without ﬁrst altering ground conditions had minimal
effect in the few cases where it was examined (ID2, 7, 8,
and 18; Table 1), except for one study where direct seeding
resulted in increased density of woody stems after 1.5 years
(ID10; Table 1). In general, there was an apparent trend for
interventions that combined manipulation of ground conditions
with actions to increase propagule supply to be most consistent
in promoting positive progress toward restoring forest struc-
ture (ID1, 2, 8, and 10; Table 1). This general pattern remains
evident even after accounting for the potential confounding
inﬂuence of the duration of intervention (Fig. 3).
disposition: Dry/rain differences and combined treatment patterns are context-specific efficacy, not rainfall gates. ID10positive seeding1.5years; unlike controls/response variables prevent pooled T4 conversion.

label: Richness outcomes
quote:
Richness.
Suppression of herbaceous vegetation through
cutting positively affected species richness of broadleaved
seedlings in pasture (ID8; Table 1). At a bracken dominated
site, cutting increased seedling species richness, but most
were perennial herbs with few forest tree species; addition of
bracken root removal and tilling treatments further increased
richness, but again mainly of perennial herbs (ID17; Table 1).
Follow-up secondary treatments are also likely to be important
in governing outcomes of interventions, but there were too
few data in the studies reviewed here to test their independent
effects.
disposition: Broadleaved seedlings vsperennial herbs distinguished; ID8/17. Secondary follow-up effects not independently testable. Effect pointer.

label: Discussion continuation
quote:
Discussion
Effectiveness of Low-Intensity Interventions
Most interventions aimed at alleviating ground conditions

label: Discussion ground interventions
quote:

structure and richness. Greatest effects were evident in a study
that showed that increase in woody seedling abundance after
1.5 years followed removal of all grasses and other plants and
tilling soil to a depth of 10 cm in a human-induced grassland
in Sri Lanka (Gunaratne et al. 2010). Cutting of standing
vegetation in an abandoned pasture in southern Costa Rica
increased cover and richness of broadleaved species 6 months
after treatment (Holl et al. 2000). Two studies reported
negative outcomes with respect to restoration goals: a study
of dry forest in central Brazil where mechanized tilling of soil
reduced the density of naturally regenerating trees resprouting
from roots (Sampaio et al. 2007), and a study from Eastern
Amazonia where fertilizer addition after burning ultimately
resulted in increased grass cover (Gehring et al. 1999).

label: Discussion combined interventions
quote:
Two main interventions have been employed to increase
propagule supply: direct seeding and artiﬁcial bird perches.
However, these interventions have met with mixed success
in terms of promoting the return of forest structure. A
combination of interventions to increase propagule supply and
to suppress herbaceous vegetation has been more effective
than either intervention used alone (Holl et al. 2000; Posada
et al. 2000; Brooks et al. 2009; Ammondt et al. 2013),
consistent with the notion that tropical forest trees can be
both dispersal and establishment limited (Holl 2012). This
ﬁnding implies that multiple types of barriers to succession
likely need to be simultaneously overcome to achieve tangible
restoration progress (Reid & Holl 2013). It is surprising
then that combined interventions have not been tested more
frequently or implemented on larger spatial scales.
disposition: Propagule enhancement plus herb suppression often more effective; practical treatment recipe, not pre-intervention suitability direction. Holl2000/Posada2000/Brooks2009/Ammondt2013 retained.

Limitations and Information Gaps
A broad array of strategies other than active tree planting has
emerged during the past two decades, to stimulate regeneration
of tropical forest on degraded land. Furthermore, there is a
growing effort in this space, with most of the studies evaluated

label: Limitations knowledge
quote:
in this review having been published within the last 10 years
(Table 1). Unfortunately, however, we ﬁnd that the state of
scientiﬁc knowledge has not yet progressed to a stage whereby
it is possible to generalize outcomes of speciﬁc interventions
relative to tree planting. It is therefore timely to identify
promising directions in which to direct future experimental

disposition: Cannot generalize intervention outcomes relative to planting; authors explicit.

label: Limitations design
quote:
This review revealed several common limitations of exper-
imental design or data quality, which also impeded general
conclusions. In terms of design, few studies have conducted
manipulative experiments over areas greater than a single
hectare, and many were much smaller. There is a need for
more experimentation closer to the scale of applied restoration
projects. No study exceeded 3 years’ duration following initial
intervention, which severely limits any comparative evalua-
tion of sites’ trajectories following different interventions. It
also precludes meaningful assessment of how much secondary
treatment is needed. Half of the studies lacked a “do noth-
ing” control, which is needed to enable comparisons of the
effectiveness of interventions across studies. Some treatment
combinations were poorly represented in the studies reviewed,
which means that interactions between different types of inter-
vention remain very poorly understood—a major deﬁciency if
combined interventions are most effective. Targeted gap ﬁlling
or better incorporation of factorial experimental designs would
be helpful in addressing this deﬁciency.
disposition: Smallplots/shortduration/lackcontrols/factorial gaps; recommendations, not measured extension/governance barrier.

label: Limitations responses
quote:
In terms of data quality, assessments of interventions’ out-
comes have predominantly made use of response variables that
describe forest structure, with scarce attention to metrics that
are richer in biodiversity information (e.g. composition or rich-
ness). In the few cases where species richness has been evalu-
ated, restoration effectiveness was difﬁcult to discern because
species information was pooled, across either disparate plant
growth forms (e.g. herbaceous vegetation, and woody plants)
or functional habitat groups (e.g. forest dependent, grassland,
and non-native species).
disposition: Richness can pool disparate lifeforms/habitat groups; do not map all richness values blindly to native-tree biodiversity.

label: Potential contextual predictors
quote:
The age or successional stage of the ecosystem at the
time of initial intervention may be important in determining
differences in subsequent effect sizes. Age and stage may show
little correlation (especially among landscapes and regions)
because in some situations unassisted regeneration in the
absence of manipulation could occur rapidly, whereas in
other situations it could be slow or arrested (Chazdon 2003).
Inherent differences in the development trajectories between
study locations could therefore be a source of variability
in the analysis, along with other well established (but still
inadequately understood) factors such as the surrounding
landscape matrix, duration of land-use phase, and duration
of abandonment phase pre-manipulation (Holl 2007). There
may also be important differences in the inﬂuence of these
factors between dry forests and rain forests (Vieira & Scariot
2006). More consistent reporting to enable consideration of
these potentially confounding variables will be needed before
drawing deﬁnitive conclusions about the relative merit of
different interventions.
disposition: Age/stage/matrix/history may confound effect sizes; hypotheses and caveats, no supported suitability directions or calibrated rules.

label: Additional techniques
quote:
Our review revealed some potentially promising low-
intensity intervention restoration techniques other than those
analyzed quantitatively (see Tables S1 & S2, Appendix S1,
Supporting Information). These either did not meet our criteria
for deriving effect sizes (replication and reporting of variance
measures) or their efﬁcacy has yet to be demonstrated experi-
mentally for tropical regions or in situations that matched our
speciﬁc context of land-use history and successional stage.
Further research into their effectiveness is warranted. The
emerging work on tree islands as reforestation foci (Holl et al.
2011) also provides promising scope for hybrid approaches
between intensive tree planting and the lower intensity inter-
ventions discussed here.
disposition: TablesS1/S2/AppendixS1 pointers; excluded-study techniques not empirically demonstrated under scope. Tree islands hybrid scope requires separate review.

label: Cost limitations
quote:
Finally, costs were reported in only 4 of 20 studies
that were quantitatively analyzed (Table S2), only 1 of
which made a comparison with the cost of tree planting
(Sampaio et al. 2007; but see also Cole et al. 2011; Kuaraksa
& Elliott 2012). There is clearly a need for more cost
accounting to better inform choices of intervention approach
to meet particular restoration goals. Such decisions may
involve complex trade-offs. For example, it is likely that
the initial cost of the low-intensity interventions considered
here would be less than for planting of nursery raised tree
seedlings (see also Rodrigues et al. 2009). However, this
lower establishment cost may be offset by a need for more
prolonged secondary treatment interventions, just as a lower
initial cost of lower density tree planting is offset by a longer
and more expensive subsequent maintenance schedule than
for high density planting (Hunt 2008; Rodrigues et al. 2009).
These ongoing interventions are largely driven by the need
to suppress aggressively competitive herbaceous vegetation
in the absence of a closed tree canopy. In order to reduce
the risk of uncertain outcomes from restoration investments
and enable the choice of cost effective intervention strategies,
future restoration experiments need to be coupled with longer
term quantitative assessments of both outcomes and costs
across a range of interventions.
disposition: Only4of20reportcost;1treeplanting comparison. Initial/ongoing tradeoff explicitly likely, not measured finance-access barrier or quantified ANR costs. SupplementS2 not acquired.

label: Practice summary
quote:
Implications for Practice
• A wide range of intervention strategies, other than
tree planting, has emerged in the past two decades
to stimulate regeneration of tropical forest in disused
agricultural land.
• However, their outcomes and costs vary greatly, and
current knowledge is insufﬁcient to enable evidence
based choices of cost effective restoration method to suit
any particular restoration goal or circumstance. Further
carefully designed restoration experiments, coupled with
longer term quantitative assessments of costs and out-
comes, are needed to ﬁll these knowledge gaps.
• On the basis of the currently available information,
interventions which suppress herbaceous vegetation (e.g.
pasture grasses) and interventions which improve the
supply of plant propagules appear to be slightly more
effective at accelerating forest regeneration if used in
combination, but are infrequently effective when either
is used alone.
